subject: History of USA
title: 2. The Thirteen Colonies and the American Revolution (1606–1783)

segments.text: Reducing the Revolution to “one tax” is the single most common error here — a strong answer combines imperial reform, constitutional ideas, colonial institutions and wartime alliance together.

New England developed town-centred farming and commerce, the middle colonies were diverse and commercially active, and the southern colonies relied heavily on plantation agriculture and enslaved labour — regional differences that continued shaping U.S. history long after independence. Elected assemblies such as the Virginia House of Burgesses gave colonists real experience in local taxation and lawmaking, so many colonists believed internal taxation required their own representatives’ consent — the constitutional principle behind “no taxation without representation,” not simply dislike of paying taxes.

items.text: The constitutional claim, rooted in colonial self-government experience, that taxation required colonists’ own consent.
Prepare causes in constitutional, economic, ideological and imperial categories; make a war timeline of only major turning points; explain why French support mattered decisively.
Do not reduce the Revolution to one tax or one slogan.
Do not ignore slavery and Indigenous land when describing colonial development.
Do not describe American victory as entirely self-produced; French support was crucial.
After the Seven Years’ War (1763), Britain sought greater colonial revenue, producing disputes over taxation and representation.
Armed conflict began at Lexington and Concord in 1775; the Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776.
The American victory at Saratoga (1777) secured a formal French alliance (1778); British defeat at Yorktown (1781) led to the Treaty of Paris (1783).
Combine imperial reform, constitutional principle, colonial institutions and wartime alliance in any causal explanation — never taxation alone.
French support was decisive, not incidental, to American victory — a fact worth stating explicitly rather than assuming self-produced success.
